summary: The note describes "The Movement Movement," a campaign launched by the Center for Health Improvement and Activity (CHIA) on September 5, 2023, that enlists celebrities to model accessible, short workouts and fight sedentary lifestyles. It covers celebrity demonstrations, an online platform for logging "movement moments," wearable tech partnerships, workplace initiatives, education efforts, and inclusivity. The hope is that visibility and practical tools will shift society toward woven-in daily movement.
one_line: CHIA's "The Movement Movement" campaign uses celebrities, apps, wearables and workplace changes to encourage active living against sedentary lifestyles.
key_facts: The Center for Health Improvement and Activity (CHIA) launched its campaign "The Movement Movement" on September 5, 2023, targeting celebrities to encourage fan bases to be active.
The campaign is compared to the ALS Ice Bucket Challenge for its reliance on social media virality.
On October 10, actress Emily Stone showcased her on-set routine with personal trainer Carlos Mendoza, stressing short, intense workouts that fit a fifteen-minute gap between shoots.
On November 14, a viral video showed Jay Carter, lead singer of the band ColdFire, doing "stairwell sprints" at a concert venue before going on stage.
CHIA's online platform launched on September 20, letting people log "movement moments" and earn badges and rewards.
Sociologist Lena DuBois says the campaign harnesses celebrity cultural currency: "if they can do it, so can I."

Maria Gonzales, CHIA's head of digital engagement, shared on November 8 the partnership with FitJourney, a wearable that tracks steps and active minutes and reminds users to move after being stationary too long.
On December 1, tech giant TechSpace announced its "Active Office Initiative," featuring a mobile-office design that encourages walking meetings and includes an employee gym.
Companies have adopted standing desks, treadmill workstations, and mandatory stretch breaks during long meetings.
Dr. Alex Rivera leads the program's education taskforce and says small efforts can ward off chronic diseases like heart conditions and diabetes.
The campaigns reach out to people with disabilities, chronic illnesses, or other conditions limiting physical activity, treating bespoke solutions as valid as gym routines.
On January 12, actor Leo Harding said, "You don't need to be a superhero to be fit... Just take it one step at a time, literally."
